ABSTRACT

Academic records are often shared through manual document exchange or institution-specific systems. These approaches can make verification slow and disclose more student information than a recipient needs. This project implements a DEPA-inspired, consent-centric academic credential exchange across three services: a Consent Manager, College A as the academic data provider, and College B as the data consumer.

The Consent Manager manages institutional identities, consent requests, field-level approvals, access grants, request lifecycle, and audit records. College A maintains student academic data and exposes scoped provider access. College B initiates requests and provides student-facing approval, rejection, history, and revocation workflows. The provider validates signed access claims and checks grant status before extracting only approved canonical fields. The institution-to-institution exchange includes an ECDH key agreement and AES-GCM utility; service assertions and access claims use signed JWTs.

Recorded backend verification totals 96 passing tests (26 Consent Manager, 42 College A, 28 College B), with zero failures, errors, or skipped tests in the available Surefire reports. At report preparation, all three backend health endpoints returned HTTP 200. These checks do not establish production readiness, throughput, or exhaustive end-to-end coverage. The project demonstrates a modular prototype for explicit consent, minimal disclosure, and verifiable academic data exchange.

Keywords: DEPA, consent management, academic credentials, data minimization, JWT, ECDH, AES-GCM, Spring Boot.

1. INTRODUCTION AND PROBLEM STATEMENT

1.1 Background

Institutions need to validate enrollment, transcripts, degrees, and other academic attributes. The source institution remains authoritative while a recipient needs reliable evidence for a defined purpose. A student-centered exchange should make the source, recipient, purpose, scope, and lifecycle of each disclosure explicit.

1.2 Problem Statement

The project addresses the need for a controlled mechanism that lets a student authorize an academic-data request without transferring an unrestricted dossier. The system identifies participating institutions, records requests and decisions, enforces approved-field scope at the provider, supports revocation, and provides an auditable workflow across separate services.

1.3 Objectives

•  Model three cooperating nodes: Consent Manager, provider (College A), and consumer (College B).

•  Support authentication and role-specific administrative and student workflows.

•  Allow consent requests with purpose and requested fields; let students approve selected fields, reject, inspect history, or revoke access.

•  Issue and validate scoped grants and signed claims; check grant status before provider disclosure.

•  Map source fields to a canonical response and return only currently authorized fields.

•  Provide operational pages, bulk student registration, health checks, and automated backend tests.

1.4 Scope and Boundaries

The delivered scope is a locally deployable academic-data sharing prototype. It is not a production accreditation platform, national identity system, or formally certified DEPA deployment. Production use requires institution-approved identity proofing, key custody, privacy/legal review, hardening, monitoring, backup, and controlled operations.

2.1 System Overview

The system has three backend services and three browser frontends. The Consent Manager is authoritative for consent and grant lifecycle. College A stores provider-side records. College B initiates requests and hosts consumer/student workflows. Service communication is HTTP-based in local development; deployments should use TLS and institution-managed secrets.

2.5 Constraints and Assumptions

•  A student identifier links the request to a provider record; reliable identity proofing is outside scope.

•  Development ports/configuration are for a trusted local environment, not internet-facing deployment.

•  CSV imports require documented headers; quoting and embedded commas need validation for arbitrary files.

•  Correct disclosure depends on consistent field identifiers and aligned signing-key registration.

3. RELATED CONCEPTS AND DESIGN RATIONALE

3.1 DEPA-Inspired Data Empowerment

The design follows the principle that individuals should authorize and control a purpose-specific flow of personal information. Consent is an explicit request and lifecycle-managed grant rather than unrestricted permission. This is an academic prototype informed by the principle, not an official DEPA certification.

3.2 Scoped Authorization and Signed Claims

The Consent Manager issues and validates authorization artifacts carrying identifiers and approved field scope. College A verifies signed claims and checks live grant status before returning data. Signed JWTs provide integrity/authenticity, not confidentiality; transport security is separately required.

3.3 ECDH and Authenticated Encryption

Both college codebases include elliptic-curve key-pair generation, ECDH shared-secret derivation, and AES/GCM/NoPadding using a 12-byte random IV and a 128-bit authentication tag. The implementation uses the first 16 bytes of the shared secret as AES-128 key material. Production use requires a reviewed KDF, explicit curve selection, context binding, strict input checks, and interoperable key lifecycle management.

3.4 Data Minimization and Mapping

Provider-side extraction uses the Consent Manager-approved field list and a provider mapping registry. The response is a canonical map rather than an unrestricted serialized student entity. College B maps aliases and key capitalization for display without exposing a raw JSON dump in the record modal.

3.5 Alternatives and Contribution

ApproachStrengthTrade-off
Email/file transferLow setup effortWeak scope control, revocation, and audit consistency.
Centralized repositorySingle integration pointConcentrates sensitive records and requires migration.
Provider + consent managerProvider retains source data; central service coordinates permission.Requires key alignment, service availability, schema mapping.

The contribution is a demonstrable modular workflow combining consent lifecycle, field-level authorization, provider-held records, revocation-aware access, and operational interfaces.

4. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND WORKFLOW

4.1 Logical Architecture

NodeResponsibilitiesLocal endpoints
Consent ManagerOrganizations/users; consent, grants, audit, bridge, key registration.API :8095; UI :3001
College A — ProviderStudent records; admin APIs; authorized field extraction.API :8081; UI :3002
College B — ConsumerRequests/retrieval; student inbox, history, approval, rejection, revocation.API :8082; UI :3003

Request flow: College B request → Consent Manager lifecycle → student decision → scoped grant and signed claim → College A live grant validation and field extraction → response to College B → consumer verification/view.

4.2 End-to-End Workflow

College B selects provider, data principal, purpose, and requested academic fields.

The Consent Manager records the request and makes it available to the student workflow.

The student approves a subset of fields or rejects the request.

On approval, the Consent Manager records the decision and creates a grant with approved scope.

The consumer submits the authorized access artifact to the provider endpoint.

College A validates signature/claims and grant identity, then asks the Consent Manager for current grant state.

If valid, the provider locates the student and extracts only supported approved fields.

College B displays mapped values and status; request/audit records support administration.

A revoked or expired grant is denied after live validation.

4.3 Trust Artifacts

ArtifactPurposeHandling
Login tokenAuthenticate portal user and apply role restrictions.Not data-access authorization.
Signed service assertionAuthenticate college service calls to consent bridge.Register/rotate keys consistently.
Scoped access claim/grantAuthorize provider request for approved fields.Verify signature, identifiers, and active grant.

4.4 Security and Failure Behavior

•  Role checks partition Super Admin, organization admin, student, and institutional operations.

•  Provider checks signed claims, grant ID, data principal, and live grant state; empty/invalid scope is denied.

•  Bridge calls use signed college assertions and registered keys; expired overlap can cause authorization errors.

•  Trusted-provider URL validation is present; production still needs network egress controls and TLS.

•  Health endpoints report process health only, not data correctness or dependency readiness.

4.5 Deployment

Three Spring Boot backends and three browser frontends are locally orchestrated by start_all.ps1. PostgreSQL is used through Spring Data JPA. College key directories were configured explicitly to avoid different working directories selecting different RSA key material. Production keys must be kept outside source control and supplied through managed secrets or a key service.

5. DATABASE DESIGN AND DATA MODEL

5.1 Persistence Approach

Backend entities are mapped through JPA and configured for PostgreSQL. The Consent Manager owns governance records; each college owns its local student/admin records. The Consent Manager is not the academic source of truth.

5.2 Principal Entities

ServiceEntity/tablePurpose
Consent ManagerorganizationsInstitution registry and metadata.
Consent ManagerusersUser identities and roles.
Consent Managerconsent_requestsPrincipal, recipient, purpose, requested fields, status.
Consent ManagerconsentsDecision, approved fields, lifecycle state.
Consent Manageraccess_grantsProvider authorization scope and lifecycle.
Consent Managerdata_requestsConsumer request/retrieval state.
Consent Manageraudit_logsSecurity and lifecycle event records.
Consent Managerconsumed_assertionsAssertion replay/lifecycle tracking.
College Astudents; college_a_adminsProvider academic data and administrator accounts.
College Bstudents; college_b_adminsConsumer-side student and administrator accounts.

5.3 Relationships and Governance

•  An organization can have multiple users; administrative access is role-scoped.

•  A request identifies the data principal and recipient and contains purpose and requested fields.

•  A consent decision captures approved fields; the resulting grant is constrained to that scope.

•  Provider disclosure is allowed only while the grant is active according to the Consent Manager.

•  Production requires retention rules, encrypted backups, least-privilege DB access, and safe logging.

Exact database credentials and real student records are intentionally omitted.

7. USER MANUAL AND OPERATIONS

7.1 Prerequisites

•  Java 17 and Maven for backend build/test operations.

•  PostgreSQL and module configuration suitable for the local environment.

•  Windows PowerShell for the supplied local startup script.

•  Institution-specific credentials and signing keys; do not reuse sample/default passwords in deployment.

7.2 Start the Local System

Open PowerShell in the repository root and review commands/configuration in start_all.ps1.

Run .\start_all.ps1 and keep process windows/logs available for diagnostics.

Check health endpoints on ports 8095, 8081, and 8082; portals use ports 3001, 3002, and 3003.

Use service-specific user accounts. After restart/key rotation, sign out and authenticate again if the session is stale.

ComponentFrontendBackend health
Consent Managerhttp://127.0.0.1:3001http://127.0.0.1:8095/health
College Ahttp://127.0.0.1:3002http://127.0.0.1:8081/health
College Bhttp://127.0.0.1:3003http://127.0.0.1:8082/health

7.3 Student Consent Flow

Sign in and open the consent inbox or pending-requests view.

Review requester, purpose, data principal, fields, and status.

Approve only necessary fields or reject; confirm the decision in consent history.

Revoke active consent when access should end; the provider checks current grant status.

7.4 Consumer Retrieval Flow

Sign in as an authorized College B operator and open the request workflow.

Select a registered provider and enter student ID, purpose, and requested fields.

Wait for student decision and active grant status before retrieval.

Review mapped values/status and use the records page for follow-up.

7.5 Bulk Registration

Use samples/college_a_students_sample.csv with headers studentId,name,email,program,cgpa and samples/college_b_students_sample.csv with studentId,name,email,department,cgpa. These files contain fictional example.org addresses. Follow the import screen’s exact field requirements.

7.6 Troubleshooting

SymptomAction
Health endpoint unavailableCheck process, port, startup logs, DB connectivity, and port conflicts.
401/403Check login, role, route permissions, and correct service identity; do not bypass authentication.
Consent bridge stale key IDCheck assertion registration and configured key directory; re-register/rotate with the supported flow.
Approved request but denied retrievalCheck approved scope, grant ID/claim match, active grant, and provider principal mapping.

8. CONCLUSION, LIMITATIONS, AND FUTURE WORK

8.1 Conclusion

The project delivers a three-service academic credential exchange prototype that places consent and approved-field scope at the center of retrieval. The Consent Manager manages request/grant lifecycle, College A remains the source of academic records, and College B provides consumer and student workflows. Backend tests and point-in-time health checks provide evidence that core modules run and recorded suites pass.

8.2 Limitations

•  Local-development prototype; no production identity proofing, deployment security review, disaster-recovery exercise, or independent penetration test is claimed.

•  Live checks cover health endpoints; exhaustive protected-route and full browser-to-provider-to-consumer verification is not claimed.

•  ECDH/AES utility uses a direct shared-secret slice for AES key material and needs a reviewed KDF/protocol before production.

•  Key registration depends on consistent key identifiers and configured directories; stale keys can interrupt bridge communication.

•  Performance, concurrency, retention, usability, and cross-institution benchmarks have not been established.

•  CSV ingestion needs further validation for quoting, malformed input, and arbitrary external files.

8.3 Future Enhancements

•  Adopt an approved KDF, protocol versioning, key confirmation, and managed key rotation.

•  Deploy TLS, managed secrets, strict CORS, network egress controls, rate limits, secure token policy, and monitoring.

•  Add browser-level end-to-end tests for request, decision, grant, retrieval, field filtering, and revocation.

•  Add schema versioning and standard credential formats across institution registries.

•  Define retention/deletion policies and test backup/restore and operational recovery.

•  Run repeatable load, concurrency, and resilience tests.
